summary.text: A synapse is a structure that lets a neuron exchange signals, by receiving or sending them, with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Synapses are either chemical or electrical, depending on how the signal is transmitted between the cells.
They are essential for passing nerve impulses from one neuron to the next, enabling rapid, direct communication by creating circuits.

facts.label: Gap width
facts.value: About 20 nanometers separate the two sides

facts.label: First clear view
facts.value: Needed an electron microscope, available only in the 1950s

facts.label: Electrical advantage
facts.value: Rapid transfer of signals from one cell to the next

items.prompt: Two neurons are joined by gap junctions. How does a voltage change in one reach the other?

options.label: A chemical messenger is released and binds to receptors
Electric current flows directly through the channels
Both cells swap their cell bodies for a moment
A third cell relays it with a slow chemical signal

items.explain: In an electrical synapse the special channels pass electric current directly, with no neurotransmitter needed.

items.prompt: One synaptic site delivers a signal with a fast part and a slow part. What does that site feature?

options.label: Neither, since it relies on indirect electric fields
Both a gap junction and neurotransmitter release

items.explain: Mixed chemical-electrical synapses have both, which gives a fast electrical component and a slow chemical one.

items.prompt: A drug makes receiving neurons less likely to fire an action potential. Which type of synapse effect does that match?
items.explain: An inhibitory synapse lowers the chance of depolarization and of an action potential in the receiving neuron.

items.prompt: A neuron's axon forms a synapse onto the dendrites of that very same neuron. What is this called?
items.explain: An autapse is a chemical or electrical synapse formed when a neuron's axon synapses onto its own dendrites.

items.prompt: A neuron's axon terminal passes a signal toward a target cell's dendrite. What is the neuron doing the passing called?
items.explain: The signal-passing neuron is the presynaptic neuron, whose membrane sits close to that of the postsynaptic target cell.

items.prompt: One neurotransmitter, acetylcholine, excites some cells and inhibits others. What decides which effect it has?

options.label: The size of the neuron that releases it
The time of day it is released
The type of receptor it binds to

items.explain: Acetylcholine can excite or inhibit depending on the type of receptors it binds to.

paragraphs.heading: A meeting point between cells
paragraphs.text: A synapse is the spot where a nerve cell, or neuron, passes signals to a neighbouring cell or takes signals in from it. The sending cell is called the presynaptic cell and the receiving one the postsynaptic cell. Their outer membranes come very close together there. On both sides sits a dense set of molecular machinery that ties the two membranes to each other and does the work of signalling.

paragraphs.heading: Why synapses matter
paragraphs.text: Nerve impulses could not travel from one neuron to the next without synapses. By linking neurons into circuits, they make quick, direct communication possible. A synapse is also more than a relay: information gets processed there as well as passed along. In many cases the sending side sits at the tip of an axon, and the receiving side sits on a dendrite or on the cell body.

paragraphs.heading: A gap too small to see
paragraphs.text: Santiago Ramón y Cajal argued that neurons are separate cells that still talk to one another, an idea called the neuron doctrine. For a long time the gap between cells stayed a theory, since the best light microscopes of the day could not resolve it; it is now known to be about 20 nm wide. Only the electron microscope, which arrived in the 1950s, revealed the two parallel membranes and the cleft lying between them.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical synapses
paragraphs.text: In a chemical synapse, electrical activity in the sending neuron opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and this leads it to release a neurotransmitter, a chemical messenger. The neurotransmitter attaches to receptors on the membrane of the receiving cell. It can trigger an electrical response there or start a chain of secondary messengers, and the result may excite or inhibit the receiving neuron. Because receptor signalling is intricate, the effects on the receiving cell can be complex.

paragraphs.heading: Electrical synapses
paragraphs.text: In an electrical synapse, the two membranes are joined by special channels called gap junctions, which let electric current pass straight through. A voltage change in one cell then causes a voltage change in the other, with no neurotransmitter needed. Small molecules such as calcium can also cross. The chief benefit is speed. The coupling runs both ways, so the direction of a signal cannot always be pinned down.

paragraphs.heading: Speeding up or holding back
paragraphs.text: An excitatory synapse makes it more likely that the receiving neuron will fire an action potential. It does this by letting Na⁺ flow in, which pushes the membrane toward the firing threshold. An inhibitory synapse does the opposite, opening Cl⁻ or K⁺ channels so that firing becomes less likely. Glutamate is an example of an excitatory neurotransmitter, while GABA works as an inhibitory one.

paragraphs.heading: Same messenger, different effect
paragraphs.text: Whether a transmitter excites or inhibits depends on where it is released, which receptors it meets, and the ions around it. Acetylcholine, for example, can do either, depending on the receptor type it binds. Dopamine likewise has both effects, acting through different receptors. So one chemical can carry opposite messages at different synapses.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word came from
paragraphs.text: The English neurophysiologist Charles Sherrington introduced the word synapse in 1897. He wanted a term that stressed a joining of two separate parts, and the classical scholar Arthur Woollgar Verrall suggested it. It comes from the Greek synapsis, meaning conjunction, built from roots meaning together and to fasten.
